findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported in SalesforceCalendarService
findings.body: The new token-refresh code in `getClient()` calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) contain no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` (unlike every other CalendarService changed in this PR). This fails type-check/build, and at runtime throws `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` the first time a Salesforce credential is used, breaking Salesforce event creation entirely.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed keys are broken and the schema strips all expiry/refresh fields
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal key "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no custom toString), so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown-optional }`. The comment claims "any property with a number is the expiry" but nothing like that is implemented — no expiry field is validated. Worse, zod's `z.object().parse` strips unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled the returned `data` contains only `access_token` (plus the dummy refresh_token injected at line 26). Callers that persist this data — Google CalendarService (`data: { key }`) and Salesforce (`data: { key: { ...accessTokenParsed.data, ... } }`) — will save credentials that have lost `refresh_token`, `expiry_date`, `instance_url`, `scope`, etc., permanently corrupting the stored credential. For Zoom, `newTokens.expires_in` is then undefined so `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + undefined * 1000)` stores NaN.

findings.title: Dummy `refresh_token = "refresh_token"` overwrites real refresh tokens, including when sync is disabled
findings.body: When the parsed token response lacks `refresh_token`, the code unconditionally sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. This is not limited to the sync-enabled path — it also runs for the normal per-app schema. Microsoft's refresh-token endpoint legitimately omits `refresh_token` on refresh responses (the existing refresh token stays valid); previously Office365CalendarService preserved the old token via `{ ...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data }`, but now the placeholder string "refresh_token" is spread over the real token and written to the DB. The next refresh will send `refresh_token=refresh_token` and fail with invalid_grant, breaking Office 365 calendar sync for existing non-sync users as a regression from this PR.

findings.title: Sync mode returns a raw fetch Response but callers expect library-specific objects (axios responses, hubspot tokens, gaxios res)
findings.body: When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` and `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set, `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the raw `fetch` `Response` object. Several callers cannot handle that: HubspotCalendarService (CalendarService.ts:177-202) treats the return as a `HubspotToken` and reads `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` (→ NaN expiryDate stored, `setAccessToken(undefined)`); zoho-bigin (CalendarService.ts:96) and zohocrm (CalendarService.ts:217) read `.data` on it (→ TypeError "Cannot set properties of undefined", crash); GoogleCalendarService (CalendarService.ts:94) reads `res?.data` from what used to be a gaxios response (`fetchTokens.res`), which is undefined on a fetch Response → `token.access_token` throws. Enabling the advertised sync feature breaks these apps outright; each caller needs the sync response normalized into the shape it expects.

findings.title: Salesforce connection is built with the stale access token after refreshing, and refresh now runs on every use
findings.body: In `getClient()`, a new access token is fetched via the token endpoint and persisted to the DB (lines 75-99), but the `jsforce.Connection` returned at line 101 is constructed with `accessToken: credentialKey.access_token` — the *old* token read from the credential before the refresh. The newly obtained `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token` is never used, so API calls run against the stale (possibly expired) token. Additionally, unlike the other services, there is no expiry check: `getClient()` is called from the constructor on every service instantiation, so every booking operation now performs a Salesforce token refresh and a DB write even when the stored token is still valid. The `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` check at line 92 is also dead code since `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws on failure.

findings.title: zoho-bigin passes credentialId as the userId argument to refreshOAuthTokens
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(refreshFn, "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` sends the *credential* id where the function's third parameter is `userId` and is transmitted to the sync endpoint as `calcomUserId`. In credential-sync mode the parent application receives the wrong identifier, so it will look up the wrong user's tokens (or none), breaking token refresh for Zoho Bigin whenever sync is enabled. The correct value is `credential.userId`, as used by all other apps.

findings.title: Webhook handler: uncaught ZodError/decrypt/JSON.parse errors return 500, no method check, and decrypted keys stored unvalidated
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError on malformed input, and `symmetricDecrypt`/`JSON.parse` (line 57) throw on bad ciphertext or non-JSON plaintext — none are caught, so the caller gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx. The handler also never checks `req.method`, so it mutates credentials on GET/PUT/etc. Finally, the decrypted `keys` object is written straight into `credential.key` without validating it against the target app's credential schema (e.g. `googleCredentialSchema`), so arbitrarily-shaped JSON can be persisted and will only fail later inside the app's service code.

findings.title: Credential update does not clear the `invalid` flag and may clobber the wrong credential
findings.body: When updating an existing credential (line 73), the `invalid` field is not reset to false, so if the credential was previously marked invalid (e.g. after an invalid_grant), syncing fresh valid keys leaves it permanently disabled. Additionally, `findFirst` on `{ userId, appId }` picks an arbitrary record when a user has multiple credentials for the same app slug (Cal.com supports multiple installed credentials per app per user, e.g. multiple Google accounts), so the new keys can overwrite the wrong account's tokens.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with plain !== instead of constant-time comparison
findings.body: The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses ordinary string comparison, which is not constant-time and leaks timing information about the secret's length/prefix to an attacker probing the endpoint. Since this secret authorizes writing arbitrary OAuth credentials for any user id, the comparison should use a constant-time equality check (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers).

findings.title: No tests for the new OAuth sync helpers or the credential webhook
findings.body: The PR introduces a new unauthenticated-surface webhook endpoint, a global switch that changes the token-refresh code path of ten apps, and schema/parse helpers with non-trivial behavior — and the PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. Given that several of these paths are broken as written (dummy refresh_token injection, schema stripping, fetch-Response type mismatches), unit tests for `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (both modes) and `refreshOAuthTokens`, plus an integration test for `/api/webhook/app-credential`, would have caught these regressions and are needed before merge.
